1	\paragraph{The epoch confound in D\&R evaluation.}
2	The bulk of D\&R's reported PPL advantage over adaptive reweighting (${>}$95\%) is attributable to multi-epoch exposure rather than filtering quality (\S\ref{sec:main-results}).
3	An independent-LR replication (D\&R $17.651$ vs.\ shared-schedule $17.657$, $\Delta{=}0.006$) confirms that this finding is robust to LR schedule choice.
4	D\&R evaluations that do not control for content epochs systematically overstate filtering effectiveness; the residual benefit ($\Delta{=}0.017$ vs.\ adaptive $\bstar$, directionally consistent across 3 seeds) falls within cross-seed variance.
5	A permuted-score control (shuffled detector scores; 3-seed mean $17.951{\pm}0.007$, $+$0.26 vs.\ uniform) confirms that detector signal is load-bearing: uninformed reweighting only degrades.
6	
7	\paragraph{When uniform beats reweighting.}
8	Beyond the evaluation confound, our results identify three operational conditions for effective reweighting, each of which, when violated, makes uniform training preferable.
9	First, \emph{detector quality}: the detector must provide both sufficient discrimination (AUC) and good calibration (ECE).
10	A high-AUC but poorly calibrated detector (GPT-2, ECE\,=\,0.131) degrades PPL by $+$0.098 below uniform; even a well-calibrated detector with insufficient discrimination (N-gram, AUC\,=\,0.73) degrades by $+$0.129 (\S\ref{sec:robustness}).
11	Second, \emph{contamination level}: at $\rho{=}0.2$, the detector's signal-to-noise ratio is too low and the method actively intervenes on unreliable signal ($\aeff$-binding at 60.1\% despite mean $q{=}0.393$), degrading PPL by $+$0.046.
12	Third, \emph{scale}: at 1.7B the benefit diminishes ($\Delta{=}{-}0.013$) with OOD partially inconsistent, suggesting that larger models may be inherently more robust to contamination generated by smaller models.
13	In all three failure cases, the adaptive method's dual constraint limits degradation relative to unconstrained reweighting (ESS-only), but uniform remains the safer default when conditions are uncertain (Table~\ref{tab:decision}).
14

18	\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}

21	\toprule

24	Detector AUC $\geq 0.9$ & Yes & N-gram (0.73) degrades & $+$0.129 \\
25	Detector ECE $\leq 0.05$ & Yes & GPT-2 (0.131) degrades & $+$0.098 \\
26	Contamination $\rho \geq 0.4$ & Yes & $\rho{=}0.2$ degrades & $+$0.046 \\
27	Generator $\neq$ trainee & Rec. & 1.7B: $\Delta{=}{-}0.013$, OOD mixed & --- \\
28	\bottomrule
29	\end{tabular}}

36	\paragraph{Downstream tasks do not reflect PPL improvements.}
37	The boundary conditions above frame the practical significance of the observed improvements.
38	Despite consistent holdout PPL improvements across seeds ($\Delta{=}{-}0.020$ at $\rho{=}0.4$), downstream benchmark accuracy is identical between adaptive and uniform training (Table~\ref{tab:downstream_main}).
39	Across three seeds, the mean accuracy difference is ${\leq}0.001$ with mixed directionality; no individual task shows a consistent advantage.
40	This null result is informative: it suggests that the PPL improvements from contamination-aware reweighting operate in a regime that standard benchmarks cannot resolve.
41	Quantitatively, $\Delta{=}{-}0.020$ PPL corresponds to ${\sim}$0.1\% relative improvement; on 5-choice tasks with ${\sim}$1{,}000 evaluation items, each question contributes ${\sim}$0.001 to accuracy, so the expected accuracy change from a 0.1\% PPL shift is far below per-task measurement noise ($\sigma \approx 0.01$).
42	More broadly, the relationship between pretraining perplexity and downstream accuracy is nonlinear and scale-dependent~\citep{tay2023scale}: small PPL gains at 0.6B may not cross the threshold where downstream metrics begin to respond, consistent with findings in data mixing~\citep{ye2025mixing} where optimized mixtures similarly fail to transfer at smaller scales.

52	Mean $|\Delta|$ per task & \multicolumn{2}{c}{$\leq$ 0.01} \\
53	Direction & \multicolumn{2}{c}{mixed across seeds} \\
54	\bottomrule
55	\end{tabular}
56	\caption{Downstream benchmark summary ($\rho{=}0.4$, 5 tasks, 3 seeds; per-task details in Appendix~\ref{app:downstream}).

58	\label{tab:downstream_main}

61	\paragraph{Effect size in context.}
62	These results raise the question of whether the observed improvements justify the method's overhead.
63	The in-distribution PPL improvement from adaptive reweighting ($\Delta{=}{-}0.020$ at $\rho{=}0.4$) operates within a narrow residual: continued pretraining absorbs ${\sim}$5 PPL points of easy gains (22.97 $\to$ 17.69), leaving method comparisons to operate within a ${\sim}$0.07-point window between uniform and grid-best (0.18 across all methods including random).
64	After accounting for the epoch confound, the true value added by detect-and-reweight is substantially smaller than published results suggest.
65	This finding is itself valuable: the detect-and-reweight paradigm's practical impact at current scales is modest, and practitioners should weigh the method's computational cost (detector training, per-batch $b^{*}$ computation) against the expected gain.
66	At $\rho{=}0.6$ the effect roughly doubles ($\Delta{=}{-}0.032$), suggesting that the method's value may increase as web contamination grows---but this extrapolation is speculative.
67	
68	\paragraph{Limitations of $\aeff$ as a proxy.}
69	The $\aeff$ diagnostic correlates with the true batch-level real fraction at Pearson $r \approx 0.70$, explaining ${\sim}$49\% of variance (Appendix~\ref{app:alpha_validation}).
70	The proxy correlation is stable across seeds: $r(\aeff, \bar{q}) = 0.80 \pm 0.001$ (cross-seed spread ${<}$0.003, Spearman $\rho > 0.87$; Table~\ref{tab:alpha_corr_perseed}).
71	Note that $r(\aeff, \bar{q}) = 0.80$ measures proxy-to-proxy (detector score) correlation, while $r(\aeff, \text{true real fraction}) = 0.706$ (Table~\ref{tab:alpha_corr}) measures proxy-to-ground-truth; the gap reflects thresholding noise in $r_i$, and the key information from the per-seed analysis is the cross-seed stability, not the absolute value.
72	The remaining variance arises from two sources: the binary indicator $r_i = \mathbf{1}[q_i \leq 0.5]$ discards calibration information within each half of the $q$-score range, and small batch sizes ($B{=}4$) amplify sampling noise.
73	Quantitative decomposition attributes ${\sim}$70\% of unexplained variance to detector noise (TF-IDF accuracy drops to ${\sim}$55\% in the boundary region $q \in [0.4, 0.6]$) and ${\sim}$30\% to the adaptive $\bstar$ transform, which intentionally compresses $\aeff$ toward $\tau$ via the ESS $\geq \nmin$ constraint.
74	Scaling from $B{=}4$ to $B{=}16$ reduces per-batch $\aeff$ variance by $10.25{\times}$ but leaves $R^2$ essentially unchanged ($0.47 \to 0.44$), confirming that the practical ceiling is set by detector calibration quality rather than batch size.
75	Increasing $B$ nonetheless improves the adaptive advantage monotonically ($1.0{\times}$ at $B{=}4$, $2.2{\times}$ at $B{=}8$ single seed, $3.4{\times}$ at $B{=}16$ 3 seeds; \S\ref{sec:sensitivity}), but with diminishing marginal gains ($2.2{\times}$ for the first doubling, $1.5{\times}$ for the second).
76	However, the $r{=}0.70$ correlation sets a ceiling on how precisely the method can target contamination: a better proxy (e.g., using soft $q$-scores directly rather than thresholded indicators) might improve the method's effective range, particularly at $\rho{=}0.2$ where the current proxy fails.

\paragraph{The epoch confound in D\&R evaluation.}
The bulk of D\&R's reported PPL advantage over adaptive reweighting (${>}$95\%) is attributable to multi-epoch exposure rather than filtering quality (\S\ref{sec:main-results}).
An independent-LR replication (D\&R $17.651$ vs.\ shared-schedule $17.657$, $\Delta{=}0.006$) confirms that this finding is robust to LR schedule choice.
D\&R evaluations that do not control for content epochs systematically overstate filtering effectiveness; the residual benefit ($\Delta{=}0.017$ vs.\ adaptive $\bstar$, directionally consistent across 3 seeds) falls within cross-seed variance.
A permuted-score control (shuffled detector scores; 3-seed mean $17.951{\pm}0.007$, $+$0.26 vs.\ uniform) confirms that detector signal is load-bearing: uninformed reweighting only degrades.

\paragraph{When uniform beats reweighting.}
Beyond the evaluation confound, our results identify three operational conditions for effective reweighting, each of which, when violated, makes uniform training preferable.
First, \emph{detector quality}: the detector must provide both sufficient discrimination (AUC) and good calibration (ECE).
A high-AUC but poorly calibrated detector (GPT-2, ECE\,=\,0.131) degrades PPL by $+$0.098 below uniform; even a well-calibrated detector with insufficient discrimination (N-gram, AUC\,=\,0.73) degrades by $+$0.129 (\S\ref{sec:robustness}).
Second, \emph{contamination level}: at $\rho{=}0.2$, the detector's signal-to-noise ratio is too low and the method actively intervenes on unreliable signal ($\aeff$-binding at 60.1\% despite mean $q{=}0.393$), degrading PPL by $+$0.046.
Third, \emph{scale}: at 1.7B the benefit diminishes ($\Delta{=}{-}0.013$) with OOD partially inconsistent, suggesting that larger models may be inherently more robust to contamination generated by smaller models.
In all three failure cases, the adaptive method's dual constraint limits degradation relative to unconstrained reweighting (ESS-only), but uniform remains the safer default when conditions are uncertain (Table~\ref{tab:decision}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcll@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Req'd?} & \textbf{Evidence} & \textbf{$\Delta$ PPL} \\
\midrule
Detector AUC $\geq 0.9$ & Yes & N-gram (0.73) degrades & $+$0.129 \\
Detector ECE $\leq 0.05$ & Yes & GPT-2 (0.131) degrades & $+$0.098 \\
Contamination $\rho \geq 0.4$ & Yes & $\rho{=}0.2$ degrades & $+$0.046 \\
Generator $\neq$ trainee & Rec. & 1.7B: $\Delta{=}{-}0.013$, OOD mixed & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\caption{Decision summary for practitioners.
$\Delta$ values are relative to uniform (positive = worse).
When any required condition is violated, uniform is the safer default.}
\label{tab:decision}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Downstream tasks do not reflect PPL improvements.}
The boundary conditions above frame the practical significance of the observed improvements.
Despite consistent holdout PPL improvements across seeds ($\Delta{=}{-}0.020$ at $\rho{=}0.4$), downstream benchmark accuracy is identical between adaptive and uniform training (Table~\ref{tab:downstream_main}).
Across three seeds, the mean accuracy difference is ${\leq}0.001$ with mixed directionality; no individual task shows a consistent advantage.
This null result is informative: it suggests that the PPL improvements from contamination-aware reweighting operate in a regime that standard benchmarks cannot resolve.
Quantitatively, $\Delta{=}{-}0.020$ PPL corresponds to ${\sim}$0.1\% relative improvement; on 5-choice tasks with ${\sim}$1{,}000 evaluation items, each question contributes ${\sim}$0.001 to accuracy, so the expected accuracy change from a 0.1\% PPL shift is far below per-task measurement noise ($\sigma \approx 0.01$).
More broadly, the relationship between pretraining perplexity and downstream accuracy is nonlinear and scale-dependent~\citep{tay2023scale}: small PPL gains at 0.6B may not cross the threshold where downstream metrics begin to respond, consistent with findings in data mixing~\citep{ye2025mixing} where optimized mixtures similarly fail to transfer at smaller scales.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}
\toprule
& \textbf{Adaptive} & \textbf{Uniform} \\
\midrule
Mean accuracy (3 seeds) & 0.5414 & 0.5414 \\
Mean $|\Delta|$ per task & \multicolumn{2}{c}{$\leq$ 0.01} \\
Direction & \multicolumn{2}{c}{mixed across seeds} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Downstream benchmark summary ($\rho{=}0.4$, 5 tasks, 3 seeds; per-task details in Appendix~\ref{app:downstream}).
All differences within standard error; reweighting PPL gains do not transfer to downstream accuracy at this scale.}
\label{tab:downstream_main}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Effect size in context.}
These results raise the question of whether the observed improvements justify the method's overhead.
The in-distribution PPL improvement from adaptive reweighting ($\Delta{=}{-}0.020$ at $\rho{=}0.4$) operates within a narrow residual: continued pretraining absorbs ${\sim}$5 PPL points of easy gains (22.97 $\to$ 17.69), leaving method comparisons to operate within a ${\sim}$0.07-point window between uniform and grid-best (0.18 across all methods including random).
After accounting for the epoch confound, the true value added by detect-and-reweight is substantially smaller than published results suggest.
This finding is itself valuable: the detect-and-reweight paradigm's practical impact at current scales is modest, and practitioners should weigh the method's computational cost (detector training, per-batch $b^{*}$ computation) against the expected gain.
At $\rho{=}0.6$ the effect roughly doubles ($\Delta{=}{-}0.032$), suggesting that the method's value may increase as web contamination grows---but this extrapolation is speculative.

\paragraph{Limitations of $\aeff$ as a proxy.}
The $\aeff$ diagnostic correlates with the true batch-level real fraction at Pearson $r \approx 0.70$, explaining ${\sim}$49\% of variance (Appendix~\ref{app:alpha_validation}).
The proxy correlation is stable across seeds: $r(\aeff, \bar{q}) = 0.80 \pm 0.001$ (cross-seed spread ${<}$0.003, Spearman $\rho > 0.87$; Table~\ref{tab:alpha_corr_perseed}).
Note that $r(\aeff, \bar{q}) = 0.80$ measures proxy-to-proxy (detector score) correlation, while $r(\aeff, \text{true real fraction}) = 0.706$ (Table~\ref{tab:alpha_corr}) measures proxy-to-ground-truth; the gap reflects thresholding noise in $r_i$, and the key information from the per-seed analysis is the cross-seed stability, not the absolute value.
The remaining variance arises from two sources: the binary indicator $r_i = \mathbf{1}[q_i \leq 0.5]$ discards calibration information within each half of the $q$-score range, and small batch sizes ($B{=}4$) amplify sampling noise.
Quantitative decomposition attributes ${\sim}$70\% of unexplained variance to detector noise (TF-IDF accuracy drops to ${\sim}$55\% in the boundary region $q \in [0.4, 0.6]$) and ${\sim}$30\% to the adaptive $\bstar$ transform, which intentionally compresses $\aeff$ toward $\tau$ via the ESS $\geq \nmin$ constraint.
Scaling from $B{=}4$ to $B{=}16$ reduces per-batch $\aeff$ variance by $10.25{\times}$ but leaves $R^2$ essentially unchanged ($0.47 \to 0.44$), confirming that the practical ceiling is set by detector calibration quality rather than batch size.
Increasing $B$ nonetheless improves the adaptive advantage monotonically ($1.0{\times}$ at $B{=}4$, $2.2{\times}$ at $B{=}8$ single seed, $3.4{\times}$ at $B{=}16$ 3 seeds; \S\ref{sec:sensitivity}), but with diminishing marginal gains ($2.2{\times}$ for the first doubling, $1.5{\times}$ for the second).
However, the $r{=}0.70$ correlation sets a ceiling on how precisely the method can target contamination: a better proxy (e.g., using soft $q$-scores directly rather than thresholded indicators) might improve the method's effective range, particularly at $\rho{=}0.2$ where the current proxy fails.
